text: Tests, lint, static analysis, coverage — none of that produces anything Northbridge Retail can actually run. This lesson is where storefront-api's source tree becomes a container image: one versioned artifact that runs the same on a laptop, a CI runner, and production.

Building an image costs real CI minutes — pulling a base image, installing dependencies, running docker build layer by layer — so it runs last, not first. The build-image job uses needs to wait on both test and lint, since there's no point spending that time on code that was always going to be rejected.

Here's the real Dockerfile. Stage one installs dependencies in a full Python build environment, with every compiler pip install might need. Stage two starts fresh from a minimal slim base and copies in only the installed packages and source code. Compilers and build tools never make it into the image that actually ships — smaller, faster to pull, and a smaller attack surface in production.

The build command tags the image with the exact commit SHA that triggered it. That tag is the commit — there's never a question of which source code produced a given image, now or months from now. A latest tag stays around for local convenience, but production never deploys from it directly.
Once pushed, the image lands in GitHub's own Packages feature, right in the repository's sidebar — the same repository that holds the source code now holds the exact artifact built from it.

One image landed in one place. Real pipelines produce far more than container images — test reports, build logs, deployment manifests, compiled packages. Next: artifact repositories, and where all of that actually lives long-term.
